articles.title: Trump's Medicaid cuts strip refugees and other legal immigrants of their health coverage
articles.text:
Trump’s Medicaid cuts strip refugees and other legal immigrants of their health coverage – WABE
Trump’s Medicaid cuts strip refugees and other legal immigrants of their health coverage
Donald Trump
Healthcare
Immigration
Medicaid
Trump's Medicaid cuts strip refugees and other legal immigrants of their health coverage
Medicaid
Associated Press
AP
October 10th, 2026
FILE - Pediatrician Irving Phillips examines a 16-month-old boy at a CommuniCARE+OLE clinic, June 26, 2025, in Davis, Calif. (AP Photo/Godofredo A. Vásquez, File)
New restrictions have stripped Medicaid coverage from certain legal immigrants, including refugees and victims of human trafficking, as part of broader federal changes to the health insurance program that are expected to force millions off their coverage.
The change effective Oct. 1 cut from Medicaid what is estimated to be hundreds of thousands of people who legally immigrated to the United States, many of whom work and pay taxes, in the latest Trump administration policy to target foreigners.
The move is part of sweeping changes to Medicaid under President Donald Trump’s 2025 tax cut and policy law, with many set to take effect early next year. The Medicaid changes are projected to result in 7.5 million fewer people with health insurance, according to the Congressional Budget Office’s 2025 estimate.
Advocates say that without Medicaid, people will not be able to afford private insurance and will either delay care or end up in emergency rooms, adding pressure to a strained health system. For immigrants, the cuts could be felt more acutely, compounding the effects of other administration efforts to restrict their access to public assistance as part of a broader immigration crackdown.
“This is about telling every immigrant in the United States that they are not welcome here and that they should leave,” said Ben D’Avanzo, a senior strategist at the National Immigration Law Center, which has pursued litigation against the Republican administration over its immigration agenda.
Refugees, asylum seekers, victims of human trafficking and domestic violence are among those who have lost coverage. Green-card holders were not impacted.
Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement that “immigrants must be able to support themselves without taking from overburdened benefits programs paid for by hard-working American taxpayers.”
D’Avanzo said many people who have lost coverage will likely only realize when they need medical care. But for some, the change has been felt immediately.
Dwindling supplies of lifesaving medication
In Tucson, Arizona, María Chacon has been caring for her son Jesus for almost five years since a car accident at 17 left him unable to breathe on his own. He requires a ventilator, a feeding tube and daily medication, and must be turned once every two hours to stop sores from forming. Chacon said he sometimes opens his eyes.
The family is originally from Mexico and entered the U.S. on a T visa, offered to victims of human trafficking, in 2018.
Chacon said Medicaid has helped cover almost $25,000 per month of care for her son, which includes a small stipend for her and her husband as compensation for being long-term caregivers. She said doctors have explained that even if they both worked 24 hours a day, they would not be able to cover the cost of his care.
“Since that day I haven’t been able to sleep. We haven’t been able to eat or anything. We’re wondering what we’re going to do?” Chacon said.
Jesus takes medication that Chacon estimates costs $7,000 a month. The supply runs out in mid-October. Without coverage, she does not know how her son is going to survive.
Chacon found out just days before the cuts that she was losing care. She called the state’s Medicaid offices to appeal. Although she is in the process of obtaining a green card, Medicaid coverage would only kick in five years after she is approved.
Steven Camarota, research director for the Center for Immigration Studies, a right-leaning think tank that seeks less immigration, said the administration “is trying to nibble around the edges” with the Oct. 1 cuts, finding piecemeal ways to curb immigration into the U.S.
Camarota believes the government should screen legal immigrants for income potential and education, reducing the number who might rely on public benefits once they cross the border.
“You need immigrants who are unlikely to need welfare,” he said, or those with high educational attainment.
The administration recently revived a federal rule that could deny green cards to immigrants who use public benefits that could include food stamps, Medicaid, housing vouchers and others.
Chacon believes the cuts to Medicaid coverage are part of the administration’s clampdown on immigrants. She said her son is in no condition to travel.
“I know that’s what he’s doing, but, as my son is, I couldn’t go to Mexico,” Chacon said.
Millions more will be dropped from Medicaid
Medicaid, jointly funded by states and the federal government, has become a political focal point during Trump’s second term. The president has pushed to root out what he describes as fraud in the program. In July, the administration deferred over $1 billion in Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota, claiming there was suspected fraud; critics argued the move targeted Democratic-led states.
As more people are cut from Medicaid, the federal government is predicted to reduce program spending by $911 billion, according to healthcare research nonprofit KFF.
In Arizona, officials said 29,000 legal immigrants were cut from Medicaid rolls on Oct. 1. In Florida, estimates are closer to 177,000. Overall, more than 281,000 immigrants from nine states and the District of Columbia are estimated to lose Medicaid coverage, according to KFF.
As more states implement various restrictions to coverage, 7.5 million people are expected to lose coverage by 2034, according to analysis by the Congressional Budget Office.

articles.title: Isaias causes tens of thousands of power outages in metro Atlanta
articles.text:
Isaias causes tens of thousands of power outages in metro Atlanta
BREAKING: Isaias causes tens of thousands of power outages in metro Atlanta
Extreme Weather
Metro Atlanta
Weather
BREAKING: Isaias causes tens of thousands of power outages in metro Atlanta
Extreme Weather
Patrick Saunders
| WABE
October 10th, 2026
The Atlanta neighborhood Home Park is shown on morning of Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026, as Post-Tropical Storm Isaias' effects continued to be felt. (Patrick Saunders/WABE)
Tens of thousands of households across metro Atlanta were without power Saturday afternoon as the effects of Isaias were felt across much of Georgia.
The storm weakened overnight and was no longer considered a hurricane, but flash flooding threats and the potential for tornadoes persisted Saturday as the storm moved inland across Alabama.
Over 90,000 households were without power in Georgia as of about noon Saturday, according to poweroutage.us. The bulk of the outages are in metro Atlanta, including 9,000 in Gwinnett, 7,700 in DeKalb, 5,300 in Cherokee, 4,300 in Pickens, 3,300 in Fulton, 2,700 in Hall, 2,400 in Henry, 1,600 in Clayton and 2,100 in Cobb.
Some 30 flights were canceled and another 90 were delayed at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, according to Flight Aware.
The storm has caused the postponement or cancellation of roadwork projects, school activities and notable local events across metro Atlanta on Saturday.
Isaias, now considered a post-tropical cyclone, made landfall Friday as a Category 2 hurricane, then quickly moved north through Alabama.
Early Saturday, Isaias was about 25 miles (40 kilometers) south-southwest of Montgomery, Alabama and nearly 105 miles (170 kilometers) south of Birmingham, Alabama, with maximum sustained winds of 35 mph (55 kph), the NHC said Saturday. It is expected to move into the Tennessee Valley later Saturday and Sunday.
All tropical storm and storm surge warnings have been discontinued. But forecasters warned that conditions could stir up tornadoes across parts of the Florida Panhandle and into Georgia and the Carolinas.
Isiaias threat continues through Sunday morning
A high wind warning and a flood watch remain in effect in North and Central Georgia until Sunday morning, according to the National Weather Service (NWS).
Winds of 15-25 mph and gusts up to 50 mph are expected in the area. The wind will continue to blow down trees and power lines, causing more power outages and making travel difficult.
Post Tropical Cyclone Isaias will continue to bring heavy rainfall to the area through Saturday night.
Excessive runoff from the rainfall may cause flooding of rivers, creeks, streams and other low-lying and flood-prone locations.  Flooding also may occur in poor drainage and urban areas.
“As Isaias continues to move through Georgia, we are monitoring its impacts statewide,” Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp wrote on X on Saturday morning. “This morning, I spoke with [FEMA] Administrator Hamilton to ensure we remain in close contact and are ready to respond wherever needed.”
A state of emergency remains in effect in Georgia through Oct. 15.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Voter engagement lacking from Democratic and Republican parties, say Latino leaders

Economy

Voter engagement lacking from Democratic and Republican parties, say Latino leaders
Election
Tiffany Griffith
| WABE
October 9th, 2026
Georgia is home to more than 429,000 Latinos of voting age - enough to sway the direction of any election. We speak to Angelica Razo (top), Santiago Marquez, and Leslie Palomino about their organizations' efforts to energize Latino voters for the November midterms and what their priorities are this election cycle. (UCLA/Mi Familia en Acción/Latin American Association/Poder Latinx)
Georgia is home to more than 429,000 Latinos of voting age. They saw their electorate grow by 58% between the 2016 and 2020 races — the fastest-expanding voter bloc in Georgia. Latinos also have a significant economic impact on the state.
According to Latino Community Fund Georgia⁠, they generate more than $52 billion in revenue, there are 91,000 Latino-owned businesses in the state, and their buying power grew nearly 100% since 2010.
However, some in the community believe both Democrats and Republicans have done a poor job of outreach to Latino voters within days of early voting for the midterm election. According to UnidosUS⁠, this has left 40% still undecided.
Like their community, Latinos have diverse priorities this election season: the cost of living, healthcare coverage access, immigrant rights & community dignity, education & in-state tuition access and civic engagement & voting resources.
On a special edition of “ Closer Look with Rose Scott⁠,” we speak to leaders of advocacy organizations about get out the vote efforts, including Vota Fest on Saturday, Oct. 24. in Lilburn at Plaza Las Américas and the Voz en Acción⁠ Public Education Campaign.
Our guests also share their message about engagement before, during, and after the November election.
Today’s Special Guests:
Angelica Razo, National Director of Campaigns and Programs for Mi Familia en Acción⁠
⁠Leslie Palomino, Georgia State Director for Poder Latinx⁠
⁠Santiago Marquez, CEO of the Latin American Association⁠

articles.title: Waffle House Index helps Southerners gauge a storm's severity
articles.text:
Waffle House Index helps Southerners gauge a storm's severity
The Waffle House Index helps Southerners — and FEMA — gauge a storm’s severity
Food
Weather
The Waffle House Index helps Southerners — and FEMA — gauge a storm's severity
Weather
AP
October 9th, 2026
Signage is posted on the inside windown of a Waffle House restaurant, Wednesday, March 25, 2020. (Mike Stewart/AP Photo)
Golden hash browns, gravy-smothered biscuits and crispy waffles with a hearty helping of syrup are among the classic Southern comfort foods. But when hurricanes tear through Southeastern towns, the hot meals and bold yellow signs of the local Waffle House provide another kind of comfort.
If a Waffle House stays open in town, even in a limited capacity, neighbors are reassured that the coming storm is unlikely to cause devastation. A closed location of the dependable diner chain has come to indicate impending disaster. The metric is known as the Waffle House Index.
What might sound like silly logic has become one of the most reliable ways for Southerners — and even federal officials — to gauge a storm’s severity and identify communities most in need of immediate aid.
What is the Waffle House Index?
The South’s favorite disaster authority provides an informal measure of how significantly a storm will affect or has affected a community.
A map of the chain’s over 1,900 locations, concentrated in the Southeast and mid-Atlantic, helps residents of storm-prone states assess whether they’re likely to lose power, experience severe flooding or endure other extreme conditions that might cause a resilient restaurant to close its doors. For some, it’s a telltale sign of whether they need to evacuate.
Waffle House is known not just for serving breakfast 24/7, 365 days a year, but also for its disaster preparedness. For decades, people across the South have noticed that the local Waffle House seemed to be the only business still open during a storm or the first to reopen after it passed.
The restaurant chain’s reputation for remaining open when people desperately needed a place to warm up, charge devices and grab a hot meal became a fairly reliable — albeit amusing — resource to help track recovery efforts. The company even operates its own storm center.
How does the index work?
Waffle House’s social media shares color-coded maps of its restaurant locations in certain regions that will soon be hit or are recovering from storm damage. The Federal Emergency Management Agency also offers some live tracking.
Green means the location is serving a full menu, indicating minimal damage in the surrounding area. The lights are on and the syrup is flowing.
Yellow means the restaurant is serving a limited menu, a signal that it’s pulling power from a generator and might have a low food supply. The area might not have running water or electricity, but there’s enough gas to fry up bacon for hungry customers.
Red means the location is closed, a sign of unsafe operating conditions and severe destruction to the restaurant or nearby communities.
How did the index start?
Former FEMA Administrator Craig Fugate has said he thought up the Waffle House Index while leading Florida’s emergency management efforts in 2004. He had been searching for something to eat while surveying the devastation left by Hurricane Charley and was only able to find a Waffle House serving a limited menu.
His team began to notice other open Waffle Houses in communities without power or running water. The restaurants eventually became a key feature on a color-coded map that his team provided to help the public and local officials identify where storm damage was most severe.
Fugate continued to use his color-coded map when he joined FEMA under President Barack Obama. He was the agency’s administrator in 2011 when a deadly tornado tore through the town of Joplin, Missouri. Both of the town’s Waffle Houses reportedly stayed open.
The restaurant chain’s disaster readiness is no coincidence. Seven locations were destroyed and 100 more shut down in 2005 during Hurricane Katrina, but company executives saw business skyrocket at restaurants that reopened quickly.
They soon embraced a business strategy centered around keeping their restaurants operable during and after a disaster, according to the company’s website. The chain said it has invested in portable generators, bought a mobile command center and trained employees on what they can still serve if they lose electricity.

articles.title: Metro Atlanta cancellations mount as Hurricane Isaias approaches Georgia
articles.text:
Metro Atlanta cancellations mount as Hurricane Isaias approaches Georgia
Metro Atlanta cancellations mount due to Hurricane Isaias
Extreme Weather
Local
Weather
Metro Atlanta cancellations mount due to Hurricane Isaias
Extreme Weather
Patrick Saunders
| WABE
October 9th, 2026
Updated October 9, 2026,
4:33 PM EDT
The Georgia Tech campus with the downtown skyline in the background, March 11, 2016, in Atlanta.
(AP Photo/David Goldman, File)
Weekend event cancellations in Atlanta began piling up Friday afternoon as Hurricane Isaias bears down on the Gulf Coast.
The now-Category 3 hurricane has led to the postponement or cancellation of roadwork projects, school activities and notable local events.
Atlanta Pride officials canceled Saturday’s festival in Piedmont Park, but Sunday’s festival and parade are still scheduled to take place.
“While this is an incredibly difficult decision, the safety and well-being of our community must always come first,” said Atlanta Pride Executive Director Chris McCain in a press release. “Atlanta Pride is a celebration of resilience, unity and community, and those values remain at the heart of everything we do. We are working diligently to ensure that Sunday’s festivities can move forward safely, and we look forward to coming together to celebrate Pride.”
Other event cancellations and postponements continue to roll in:
Fall Festival on Ponce: canceled for Saturday, on for Sunday
Chalktoberfest in Marietta: canceled Saturday and Sunday
Atlanta Mayor’s 5K on the Runway: canceled
Gwinnett Hispanic Latino Heritage Month celebration: canceled
19th Annual Atlanta Turkish Food Festival in Alpharetta: canceled
Wire & Wood Songrwriters Festival in Alpharetta: on for Friday, canceled for Saturday
Ormewood Park Maker’s Festival: canceled
Oakhurst Porchfest organizers say they still plan to hold Saturday’s event.
The Georgia Department of Transportation rescheduled roadwork that would have closed all lanes on I-285 in the Smyrna area this weekend. That will now take place Oct. 16-19.
Some school districts in the Atlanta area are canceling weekend activities because of the storm.
Atlanta Public Schools, DeKalb County Schools, Cobb County Schools and Marietta City Schools have canceled all events scheduled for Saturday.
Where is Hurricane Isaias now?
Hurricane Isaias is expected to make landfall Friday night between Mobile Bay on the Alabama coast and the city of Destin in the Florida Panhandle — a region known for powdery white sand beaches dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars and seafood shacks.
Dangerous conditions are expected throughout the western panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi, the National Hurricane Center said. Rain began falling along the coast Friday morning, and tropical storm conditions were expected by early afternoon.
A storm surge as high as 6 to 9 feet (1.8 to 2.7 meters) was predicted in some coastal areas, according to the hurricane center.
As of mid-morning Friday, the storm was centered about 240 miles (386 kilometers) south of Pensacola, Florida, and moving to the north-northeast, the center said.
The storm was packing 120 mph (193 kph) winds and picking up speed. Category 3 storms are considered major hurricanes and are capable of causing devastation.
Isaias, which will be the first hurricane to hit the eastern U.S. since Milton tore up the Gulf Coast of Florida in 2024, also is expected to bring heavy rain and potential flooding to much of the Southeast over the weekend, and then to parts of the Midwest and Northeast into Monday.
How will Hurricane Isaias impact Georgia?
The National Weather Service (NWS) says that conditions will deteriorate across metro Atlanta on Friday night, with significant impacts through Sunday morning.
NWS meteorologist Keith Stellman says Georgians should prepare to hunker down for a good part of the weekend.
“The heart of what we’re dealing with really starts late tonight, through Saturday into Saturday night, from a timing perspective,” he said.
NWS issued a flood watch for residents across North and Central Georgia in effect from late Friday through Sunday morning.
One to four inches of rain are expected, with localized amounts up to eight inches. Regions most at risk for potential damage include poorly drained areas, urban areas and creeks and streams prone to flash flooding.
Hurricane Isaias could also bring tornadoes to the area.
A high wind watch will also be in effect in North and Central Georgia from midnight tonight to 8 a.m. Sunday. Winds of 15-25 mph are expected, with wind gusts up to 50 mph. The winds could blow down trees and power lines, causing widespread power outages and making travel difficult.
Gov. Brian Kemp declared a state of emergency on Thursday across all 159 counties as Hurricane Isaias moved closer to Georgia.
The declaration mobilizes resources among state agencies, includes prohibitions on price gouging during the storm, and temporarily increases height, weight and length limits for commercial vehicles transporting essential supplies. The order also authorizes a call-up of 500 Georgia National Guard members to stand by if needed.
NWS  advised motorists to avoid driving through water-covered roadways, encouraging alternative routes if permissible.
In addition, residents are asked to exercise caution if they choose to continue with any outdoor plans, especially if close to rivers, creeks or streams.
The Associated Press and WABE’s Kendall Murry contributed to this report.

articles.title: Secoriea Turner's family urges Jackson to stop using her in ads
articles.text:
Secoriea Turner's family urges Jackson to stop using her in ads
Secoriea Turner’s family urges Jackson to stop using her in campaign ads
Election
Georgia Governor Race
Gun Violence
Keisha Lance Bottoms
Kids
Politics
Secoriea Turner's family urges Jackson to stop using her in campaign ads
Georgia Governor Race
Maya Homan
Georgia Recorder
October 9th, 2026
Mawuli Mel Davis (left) and Shean Williams (right), attorneys for Secoriea Turner’s family, speak at a press conference on Thursday, Oct. 8. (Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder)
The family of an 8-year-old girl who was killed during a period of civil unrest in Atlanta is urging Republican candidate for governor Rick Jackson to stop using her name and image in campaign material, calling the ads “deeply hurtful.”
Secoriea Turner was fatally shot in 2020 while riding in a vehicle near a Wendy’s where a man had been killed earlier by police. The fast food restaurant had become the site for demonstrations against police brutality and calls for social justice during Democratic nominee for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms’ tenure as mayor of Atlanta. Secoriea Turner’s death was part of a wave of violence occurring at the time that prompted the governor to call in the Georgia National Guard.
Jackson has used photos and news coverage of the event as part of his campaign rhetoric, arguing that Bottoms failed to keep Atlanta residents safe.
Family says Jackson campaign doubled down
Last week, Secoriea’s mother Charmaine Turner publicly urged Jackson to stop using her daughter’s name and image in campaign materials and sent his campaign a cease and desist letter. But attorneys who represent Turner’s family said that instead of honoring the request, the campaign doubled down, releasing a new attack ad featuring Charmaine’s screams as she called 911 after Secoriea was shot.
“Today we stand making it very, very clear that Secoriea Turner, that her death, that her image, that who she was as a beautiful 8-year-old, is not a part of any campaign property,” attorney Mawuli Mel Davis said during a Thursday press conference. “She should not be part of any political or campaign stunt. This is real pain.”
Turner’s mother declined to attend Thursday’s press conference, but she said in a statement provided through her attorneys that she would continue to fight for her daughter. In 2021, she filed a lawsuit against Bottoms and the city of Atlanta over their handling of the protests, which is still pending.
Jackson campaign defends ads
In a statement released ahead of the press conference, Jackson campaign spokesperson Garrison Douglas defended the use of Turner’s story in the campaign ads.
“We cannot imagine the immense pain the Turner family has gone through,” he said. “They are not a political talking point. They are one of the major reasons why Rick is running — so that another family does not have to experience such a devastating tragedy as a result of Keisha Lance Bottoms’ abdication of her duty.”
2026 Georgia Midterm Elections
Stay in the know with WABE’s 2026 Georgia Midterm Election page, where you can find the latest election news, important dates, voting locations, candidate info, results and more.
Shean Williams, another attorney who represents the Turner family, condemned the campaign ads as “morally irresponsible,” adding that Jackson never attempted to contact the Turner family before using Secoriea’s image.
“If it’s not a political point and he really cares about Secoriea Turner, her legacy, her image, then why hasn’t he even reached out before today, before he ran for governor?” he said. “It tells me it’s a political talking point because this is all political.”
The Bottoms campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment Thursday.
This story was provided by WABE media partner the Georgia Recorder.
